questions.question: The unit vector along the vector $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ is:

solution.key_concept: A unit vector is the vector divided by its own magnitude: $\hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$.
steps: Unit vector: $\hat{A} = \frac{3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}}{5}$, whose magnitude is exactly 1.
solution.why_not_others: Dividing by 7 adds the components instead of finding the magnitude. Dividing by 25 uses $A^2$ instead of $A$. Option (4) swaps the components, which changes the direction.
solution.common_trap: Dividing by the sum of the components, or by the square of the magnitude.
solution.time_saving_tip: Recognise the 3-4-5 triangle so the magnitude is 5 at once.

questions.question: The component of $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ along the direction of $\vec{B} = 3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ is:

solution.key_concept: The component of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$ is $\vec{A}\cdot\hat{B} = \frac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{B}$.
solution.why_not_others: 18 is the dot product without dividing by $B$. $\frac{18}{7}$ divides by $|\vec{A}| = 7$, which gives the component of $\vec{B}$ along $\vec{A}$. 7 is simply the magnitude of $\vec{A}$.
solution.common_trap: Dividing by the magnitude of the wrong vector.
solution.time_saving_tip: Always divide by the magnitude of the vector you are projecting onto.

questions.question: A vector makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the x-axis and $45^\circ$ with the y-axis. The acute angle it makes with the z-axis is:

solution.key_concept: For direction cosines, $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma = 1$.
solution.why_not_others: $75^\circ$ comes from wrongly assuming the three angles add up to $180^\circ$. $90^\circ$ would need $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta = 1$, which is not the case here. $45^\circ$ has no basis in the given data.
solution.common_trap: Treating direction angles like the angles of a triangle that sum to $180^\circ$.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A vector of magnitude 10 units can have a rectangular component of magnitude 12 units.
statements.R: A rectangular component of a vector of magnitude $A$ is $A\cos\theta$, and $|\cos\theta| \le 1$.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: A rectangular (perpendicular) component can never exceed the magnitude of the vector.
steps: A rectangular component equals $A\cos\theta$, and $|\cos\theta| \le 1$, so R is true.
The component therefore cannot exceed 10 units, so a 12-unit component is impossible and A is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) are all ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Confusing rectangular components with components along non-perpendicular directions.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The unit vector along $2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ is $\frac{2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}}{3}$, and the squares of its direction cosines add up to 1.
statements.II: The component of $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ along the direction of $\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Unit vector $= \frac{\vec{A}}{A}$; direction cosines satisfy $\sum\cos^2 = 1$; the projection is $\frac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{B}$.
steps: Statement I: the magnitude is $\sqrt{4+1+4} = 3$, so the unit vector is $\frac{2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}}{3}$.
Its direction cosines are $\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}$, and $\frac{4}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{4}{9} = 1$. Statement I is correct.
The component is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$, so Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements check out exactly, so any option marking either one as incorrect is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to divide by $\sqrt{2}$, or including the $\hat{k}$ term in the dot product with $\hat{i}+\hat{j}$.

questions.question: Two trains move on parallel tracks in opposite directions with speeds $54\ km\,h^{-1}$ and $36\ km\,h^{-1}$. The speed of one train relative to the other, in $m\,s^{-1}$, is:

solution.key_concept: For opposite directions, the relative speed is the sum of the speeds.
solution.why_not_others: 5 is the difference of the speeds (15 and 10 m/s), which applies to the same direction. 15 is the speed of one train alone. 90 is not converted to m/s.
solution.common_trap: Subtracting the speeds for opposite directions, or forgetting the unit conversion.
solution.time_saving_tip: Convert each speed first: 15 m/s and 10 m/s.

questions.question: A river 120 m wide flows at $3\ m\,s^{-1}$. A swimmer whose speed in still water is $5\ m\,s^{-1}$ wants to reach the point directly opposite the starting point. The time taken to cross is:

solution.key_concept: For the shortest path (zero drift), the swimmer heads upstream and $t = \frac{d}{\sqrt{v^2-u^2}}$.
steps: The speed across the river is $\sqrt{5^2-3^2} = 4\ m\,s^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: 24 s is the minimum-time crossing, $\frac{d}{v}$, which involves drift. 40 s divides by the river speed. 15 s divides by $v+u$.
solution.common_trap: Using $\frac{d}{v}$, which is the shortest time, not the shortest path.
solution.time_saving_tip: A 3-4-5 triangle gives the speed across immediately.

questions.question: Rain falls vertically at $6\ m\,s^{-1}$. A man walks horizontally at $2\sqrt{3}\ m\,s^{-1}$. To protect himself, he should hold his umbrella:
options: at $30^\circ$ to the vertical, tilted backward
at $60^\circ$ to the vertical, tilted forward
at $30^\circ$ to the vertical, tilted forward

solution.key_concept: The umbrella is held along the velocity of rain relative to the man, $\vec{v}_r-\vec{v}_m$.
steps: The relative velocity has a vertical component of 6 m/s downward and a horizontal component of $2\sqrt{3}$ m/s opposite to his walking direction.
The rain appears to come from the front, so he tilts the umbrella forward.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): at $30^\circ$ to the vertical, tilted forward
solution.why_not_others: Tilting backward gets the direction wrong. $60^\circ$ is the angle measured from the horizontal. Holding it vertically follows the actual rain direction, not the relative one.
solution.common_trap: Holding the umbrella along the actual direction of the rain.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Relative speed of two cars moving in the same direction at $20\ m\,s^{-1}$ and $15\ m\,s^{-1}$

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Relative speed of two cars moving in opposite directions at $20\ m\,s^{-1}$ and $15\ m\,s^{-1}$

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Ground speed of a swimmer (speed $12\ m\,s^{-1}$ in still water) heading perpendicular to a river flowing at $5\ m\,s^{-1}$

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Speed across the river of a swimmer (speed $5\ m\,s^{-1}$ in still water) taking the shortest path in a river flowing at $3\ m\,s^{-1}$

solution.key_concept: Speeds subtract for the same direction and add for opposite directions. Perpendicular velocities combine as $\sqrt{v^2+u^2}$, and the shortest-path speed across is $\sqrt{v^2-u^2}$.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) swap the same-direction and opposite-direction cases. Option (2) swaps the perpendicular-heading result with the shortest-path result.
solution.common_trap: Using $\sqrt{v^2+u^2}$ for the shortest path instead of $\sqrt{v^2-u^2}$.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about relative velocity are correct?

statements.B: Two bodies in free fall have zero relative acceleration, so their relative motion is uniform.
statements.C: A swimmer can cross a river with zero drift even when his speed in still water is less than the river speed, by heading upstream.
statements.D: For minimum crossing time, the swimmer heads perpendicular to the flow, and the downstream drift is $\frac{ud}{v}$.
statements.E: A person walking in rain should hold the umbrella along the actual direction of fall of the rain.

solution.key_concept: $\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A-\vec{v}_B$. Zero drift needs $v>u$. The umbrella follows the relative velocity of the rain.
steps: A is true: swapping A and B reverses the relative velocity.
B is true: both bodies have acceleration $g$, so their relative acceleration is zero.
C is false: zero drift requires $\sin\theta = \frac{u}{v} \le 1$, i.e. $v>u$.
D is true: $t = \frac{d}{v}$ and the drift is $\frac{ud}{v}$.
E is false: the umbrella must be held along the velocity of rain relative to the person.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (3) include the false statements C or E. Option (1) leaves out the true statement D.
solution.common_trap: Believing zero drift is always possible by heading upstream.

questions.question: The position of a particle is $\vec{r} = 3t\hat{i}+2t^2\hat{j}$ (in SI units). Its velocity at $t = 2$ s is:

solution.key_concept: $\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$, taken component by component.
solution.why_not_others: $6\hat{i}+8\hat{j}$ is the position at $t = 2$ s, not the velocity. $3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ uses $2t$ in place of $4t$ for the y-component. $4\hat{j}$ is the acceleration.
solution.common_trap: Substituting $t$ into $\vec{r}$ instead of differentiating.

questions.question: A particle starts from the origin with velocity $4\hat{i}\ m\,s^{-1}$ and has constant acceleration $2\hat{j}\ m\,s^{-2}$. The equation of its path is:

solution.key_concept: Write $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ separately, then eliminate $t$.
solution.why_not_others: $\frac{x^2}{8}$ comes from dropping the $\frac{1}{2}$ in $\frac{1}{2}at^2$. $\frac{x^2}{4}$ uses $t = \frac{x}{2}$. $y = \frac{x}{2}$ is a straight line, which is wrong because the acceleration is perpendicular to the initial velocity.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in the displacement equation.

questions.question: A particle has initial velocity $(2\hat{i}-3\hat{j})\ m\,s^{-1}$ and constant acceleration $(\hat{i}+3\hat{j})\ m\,s^{-2}$. Its speed at $t = 2$ s is:

solution.key_concept: $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0+\vec{a}t$ applies component-wise for constant acceleration.
solution.why_not_others: 3 m/s comes from $\vec{v}_0+\vec{a}$, which forgets to multiply by $t$. 7 m/s adds the components arithmetically. $\sqrt{13}$ m/s is the initial speed.
solution.common_trap: Adding components directly instead of using $\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In two-dimensional motion, the acceleration of a particle need not be along its velocity.
statements.R: The component of acceleration perpendicular to the velocity changes the speed of the particle.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Tangential acceleration changes speed; normal acceleration changes direction.
steps: A is true: in a plane, the acceleration can point in any direction relative to the velocity.
R is false: the perpendicular component changes the direction of motion, not the speed.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options (1), (2) and (4) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the roles of the tangential and normal components.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: For a particle with $x = 2t$ and $y = 4t-t^2$ (in SI units), the velocity at $t = 2$ s is zero.
statements.II: For the same particle, at $t = 2$ s the acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Differentiate each component separately. A zero y-velocity does not mean zero velocity.
steps: $\vec{v} = 2\hat{i}+(4-2t)\hat{j}$. At $t = 2$ s, $\vec{v} = 2\hat{i} \neq 0$, so Statement I is incorrect.
$\vec{v}\cdot\vec{a} = 0$ at $t = 2$ s, so the two are perpendicular and Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I ignores the constant x-velocity, so options (1) and (3) fail. Statement II is verified true, so option (2) fails.
solution.common_trap: Setting only $v_y = 0$ and concluding that the whole velocity is zero.

questions.question: A ball is projected with a speed of $20\ m\,s^{-1}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Its time of flight on level ground is ($g = 10\ m\,s^{-2}$):

solution.key_concept: $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$.
solution.why_not_others: 1 s is only the time to reach the top. 3.46 s uses $\cos30^\circ$ instead of $\sin30^\circ$. 4 s leaves out $\sin\theta$ altogether.
solution.common_trap: Using $\cos\theta$ for the vertical component.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at an angle $\theta$ with $\tan\theta = \frac{4}{3}$, and its horizontal range is 120 m. Its maximum height is:

solution.key_concept: $\frac{H}{R} = \frac{\tan\theta}{4}$.
solution.why_not_others: 30 m uses $R = 4H$, which holds only at $45^\circ$. 160 m forgets to divide by 4. 22.5 m uses $\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}$.
solution.common_trap: Applying $R = 4H$ at every angle.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use the ratio $\frac{H}{R}$ directly; there is no need to find $u$.

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally at $15\ m\,s^{-1}$ from the top of a 45 m high tower. The horizontal distance from the foot of the tower to where it lands is ($g = 10\ m\,s^{-2}$):

solution.key_concept: For horizontal projection, $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ and $R = ut$.
solution.why_not_others: 31.8 m uses $t = \sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$. 67.5 m uses $t = \frac{h}{g}$. 135 m uses $t = \frac{2h}{g}$ without the square root.
solution.common_trap: Dropping the factor 2 or the square root in the time of fall.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Speed of a projectile at its highest point (launch speed $u$, angle $\theta$)

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Magnitude of the acceleration at the highest point

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Maximum horizontal range for launch speed $u$

solution.key_concept: At the top, $v = u\cos\theta$ and $a = g$. At $45^\circ$, $H = \frac{u^2}{4g}$ and $R_{max} = \frac{u^2}{g}$.
steps: A: only the horizontal velocity remains, $u\cos\theta$, so A-II.
B: the acceleration is still $g$, so B-III.
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (4) swap the height at $45^\circ$ with the maximum range. Options (3) and (4) swap the speed and acceleration at the top.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the speed or the acceleration is zero at the top.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about projectile motion are correct?

statements.A: Projectiles launched with the same speed at complementary angles have equal ranges.
statements.B: At the highest point, the velocity is perpendicular to the acceleration.
statements.C: The kinetic energy at the highest point is $K\cos^2\theta$, where $K$ is the initial kinetic energy.
statements.D: For horizontal projection from a height, the time of fall increases with the horizontal speed.
statements.E: The range equals the maximum height when the angle of projection is $45^\circ$.

solution.key_concept: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. At the top only $u\cos\theta$ remains.
steps: B is true: at the top the velocity is horizontal and $g$ acts vertically.
D is false: $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ does not depend on $u$.
E is false: at $45^\circ$, $R = 4H$; $R = H$ only when $\tan\theta = 4$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: Options (2), (3) and (4) each include the false statement D or E.
solution.common_trap: Believing that a faster horizontal throw stays in the air longer.
